To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
emotional modulation of early visual cortical activity can be demonstrated by functional near-infrared imaging.
the visual cortex holds a representation of stimulus saliency, and that the processing of positive pictures is characterized by reduced haemodynamic peak latencies.
Emotional content of pictures modulates amplitude and latency of haemodynamic responses in the early visual area.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the question of how emotional information is processed in the visual cortex.
how the human brain processes emotional stimuli, particularly the role played by the amygdala and the early visual cortex in this process.
the neural mechanisms underlying emotional effects on sensory processing and their implications for the perception and evaluation of emotional stimuli.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
emotional modulation of visual cortical activity is not only possible, but that it occurs on a very early level of processing.
emotional modulation of early visual cortex is not only possible but that it occurs.
emotional modulation of visual cortex is a function of the emotional state of the observer, the emotional valence of the stimulus and the interaction between these two factors.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the early visual system is involved in the processing of emotional pictures, which is reflected by the modulation of haemodynamic response peaks.
emotional pictures can modulate the haemodynamic response in the early visual area and the modulation is related to the emotional content of the pictures.
emotional pictures modulate early visual cortex activity, and the modulation of activity is dependent on the valence of the pictures.
The main takeaway from our work is that
emotional modulation is a fundamental property of the human visual system.
emotional content modulated amplitude of haemodynamic responses and peripheral autonomic reactions, and that positive pictures induced faster haemodynamic responses than negative pictures.
the early visual system is sensitive to the emotional content of the stimuli.
